title: Git init and the .git folder
idea: `git init` turns a folder into a repository by creating a hidden `.git` folder. That folder holds the history and settings; your files stay outside it.

analogy.text: A desk with a filing cabinet beside it. The desk holds today's pages; the cabinet keeps every earlier version.
analogy.breaks: `.git` sits inside the folder, so copying or deleting the folder takes it too.

points: `git init` creates `.git` in the current folder. Nothing else changes.
`HEAD` names the current branch, which does not exist until the first commit.
Git finds the repository by looking for `.git` here, then in each parent folder.
Git calls new files untracked: no commit holds them yet. `git add` fixes that.

code.title: A new repository
code.caption: Real Git output. The last command runs in a subfolder, yet Git still finds the repository.

walk.text: Make a folder with one file. It is not a repository yet.
`-b main` names the first branch. Git creates `.git` and says so.
Your file and `.git` sit side by side. The second `ls` lists Git's own files inside `.git`.
`HEAD` points at `main`, a branch with no commits yet.
`README.md` is untracked, and `git log` has no commits to list.
From a subfolder, Git walks up to the folder that holds `.git`.

pitfalls: Run `git status` before `git init`. If it works, you are already inside a repository.
Do not run `git init` in your home folder; `git status` would list everything inside it.
Deleting `.git` erases this copy of the history. Your files stay, untracked.

quiz.q: What does the second command print?
quiz.why: `HEAD` stores the name of the current branch as a reference, even before that branch has a commit.

takeaway: A repository is your files plus `.git`, and `git init` creates the second part.
